question: A partial data path of a processor is given in the figure, where [latex]RA[/latex], [latex]RB[/latex], and [latex]RZ[/latex] are 32-bit registers. Which option(s) is/are CORRECT related to arithmetic operations using the data path as shown? ![Image](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODdhAQABAPAAAMPDwwAAACwAAAAAAQABAAACAkQBADs=) ![Image](https://practicepaper.in/wp-content/uploads/GATE/CS/20251/q17.webp)
options: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two registers.
The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.
The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two immediate values.
The data path can only implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: The given data path consists of: - Two 32-bit registers: RA and RB . - Two multiplexers ( Mux_A and Mux_B ). - Each multiplexer can select either: - the corresponding register value, or - a 32-bit immediate value. - The selected inputs are fed to the ALU, whose output is stored in register RZ . Thus, the ALU can receive the following combinations of operands: Mux_A Mux_B Operands RA RB Two registers RA Immediate One register + one immediate Immediate RB One immediate + one register Immediate Immediate Two immediate values Now, evaluate each statement. Option A: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two registers. Since Mux_A can select RA and Mux_B can select RB , the ALU can perform operations such as[latex] RZ \leftarrow RA + RB [/latex] Hence, Option A is Correct. Option B: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value. Examples: [latex] RZ \leftarrow RA + 10 [/latex]or[latex] RZ \leftarrow 20 + RB [/latex] Therefore, Option B is Correct. Option C: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two immediate values.Both multiplexers can independently select their immediate inputs. Therefore, the ALU can perform operations like[latex] RZ \leftarrow 15 + 25 [/latex] Hence, Option C is Correct. Option D: The data path can only implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.This is false because the data path also supports: - Register + Register - Immediate + Immediate - Register + Immediate Therefore, Option D is Incorrect. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460063/gate-cse-2025-set-1-question-17#a_list)

question: Which one of the following protocols may need to broadcast some of its messages?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is used by a host to automatically obtain an IP address (and other network configuration) when it first joins a network — since the host doesn't yet have an IP address (or know the server's address), its initial "DHCP Discover" message must be broadcast on the local network so that any DHCP server present can respond. [latex]\text{SMTP}[/latex] (mail), [latex]\text{FTP}[/latex] (file transfer), and [latex]\text{HTTP}[/latex] (web) are all conventional client-server protocols that communicate with a specific, already-known server address over a normal unicast connection — they have no inherent need to broadcast. Answer: DHCP Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523134/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-12#a_list)

question: Which of the following statements is/are true with respect to the interaction of a web browser with a web server using HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex]?
options: HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates downloading multiple objects of the same webpage over the same TCP connection, if the objects are stored in the same server
HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates downloading multiple objects of the same webpage over the same TCP connection, even if they are stored in different servers
HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates sending a request for downloading one object without waiting for a previously requested object to be downloaded completely
HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates downloading multiple webpages on the same server to be downloaded over a single TCP connection
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections and pipelining over a single TCP connection: - True: Multiple objects of the same webpage, if hosted on the same server, can be fetched over one persistent TCP connection — this is exactly the point of persistent connections. - False: A single TCP connection is between one client and one specific server; objects stored on a different server require a separate TCP connection to that server. So this statement is false. - True: HTTP/1.1 supports pipelining — a client can send a new request before the response to a previous request has been fully received, over the same connection. - True: Since the TCP connection persists (is not closed after one request/response), multiple different webpages/resources from the same server can be downloaded over that same single connection, one after another. Answer: Statements 1, 3, and 4 are true (same-server multi-object download, pipelining, multiple pages over one connection); statement about different servers over the same connection is false. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523071/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-9#a_list)

question: Consider an array [latex]A[/latex] of integers of size [latex]n[/latex]. The indices of [latex]A[/latex] run from [latex]1[/latex] to [latex]n[/latex]. An algorithm is to be designed to check whether [latex]A[/latex] satisfies the condition given below. [latex]\forall i, j \in\{1, \ldots, n-1\}[/latex] such that [latex]i>j,(A[i+1]-A[i])>(A[j+1]-A[j])[/latex] Which one of the following gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm that can be designed for the problem?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: The condition says: for every pair of indices [latex]i>j[/latex] (both in [latex]\{1,\ldots,n-1\}[/latex]), the consecutive difference [latex]D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i][/latex] must exceed [latex]D[j]=A[j+1]-A[j][/latex]. In other words, the sequence of consecutive differences [latex]D[1],D[2],\ldots,D[n-1][/latex] must be strictly increasing (array [latex]A[/latex] is "convex"). This can be checked with a single linear pass: compute each [latex]D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i][/latex] and verify [latex]D[i]>D[i-1][/latex] for each consecutive pair, stopping early with "no" the first time this fails. This takes [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] time, and it's optimal since every element of the array must be examined at least once to certify the condition holds. Answer: [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523118/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-28#a_list)
subject: Algorithms

question: Consider the following functions, where [latex]n[/latex] is a positive integer. [latex] n^{1 / 3}, \log (n), \log (n!), 2^{\log (n)} [/latex] Which one of the following options lists the functions in increasing order of asymptotic growth rate? Note: Assume the base of log to be [latex]2[/latex].
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: Simplify each function's asymptotic growth (using [latex]\log[/latex] base [latex]2[/latex]): - [latex]\log(n)[/latex]: grows the slowest of all — sub-polynomial. - [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex]: a polynomial with a small (fractional) exponent, grows faster than any power of [latex]\log n[/latex] but slower than [latex]n[/latex] itself. - [latex]2^{\log(n)}=n[/latex] (since exponentiating base [latex]2[/latex] by [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] simply recovers [latex]n[/latex]) — so this grows exactly like [latex]n[/latex], faster than [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex]. - [latex]\log(n!)[/latex]: by Stirling's approximation, [latex]\log(n!)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex], which grows faster than plain [latex]n[/latex] (and hence faster than [latex]2^{\log n}=n[/latex]). So the increasing order is: [latex]\log(n) \;<\; n^{1/3} \;<\; 2^{\log(n)} \;<\; \log(n!)[/latex]. Answer: log(n), n^(1/3), 2^log(n), log(n!) Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523132/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-14#a_list)

question: Consider a system with [latex]1[/latex] MB physical memory and a word length of [latex]1[/latex] byte. The system uses a direct mapped cache, with block numbers starting from [latex]0[/latex]. The word with physical address [latex]\text{0xA2C28}[/latex] is mapped to the cache block number [latex]176_{10}[/latex]. The maximum possible size of the cache (in KB ) for this configuration is ________. (answer in integer) Note: [latex]1 {~K}=2^{10}[/latex] and [latex]1 {M}=2^{20}[/latex]
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: Physical address [latex]0\text{xA2C28}[/latex] in [latex]20[/latex]-bit binary is [latex]10100010110000101000[/latex] (since [latex]1[/latex] MB [latex]=2^{20}[/latex] bytes). We're told this maps to cache block index [latex]176=10110000_2[/latex] ([latex]8[/latex] bits). To maximize the cache size, we want to find offset width [latex]b[/latex] and index width [latex]L[/latex] (cache size [latex]=2^{b+L}[/latex] bytes) such that the [latex]L[/latex]-bit field of the address immediately above the [latex]b[/latex]-bit offset exactly equals [latex]176[/latex], while making [latex]b+L[/latex] as large as possible (equivalently, keeping the remaining tag field as short as possible, but non-zero, since it must still be consistent with the given index value's exact bit-pattern). Checking all valid alignments of the address's bits, the largest working combination is offset [latex]b=6[/latex] bits (block size [latex]64[/latex] bytes) and index [latex]L=11[/latex] bits ([latex]2048[/latex] lines), which correctly extracts index [latex]=00010110000_2=176[/latex] and leaves a [latex]3[/latex]-bit tag ([latex]101_2[/latex]) — consistent with the [latex]20[/latex]-bit address ([latex]3+11+6=20[/latex]). Maximum cache size [latex]=2^{b+L}=2^{17}=131072[/latex] bytes [latex]=128[/latex] KB. Answer: 128 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523100/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-46#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: Consider a system with a processor and a [latex]4[/latex] KB direct mapped cache with block size of [latex]16[/latex] bytes. The system has a [latex]16[/latex] MB physical memory. Four words [latex]{P}, {Q}, {R}[/latex], and S are accessed by the processor in the same order [latex]10[/latex] times. That is, there are a total of [latex]40[/latex] memory references in the sequence [latex]{P}, {Q}, {R}, {S}, {P}, {Q}, {R}, {S}, \ldots[/latex] Assume that the cache memory is initially empty. The physical addresses of the words are given below ([latex]1[/latex] word [latex]=1[/latex] byte). [latex]\text{P: 0x845B32, Q: 0x845B26, R: 0x845B36, S: 0x846B32}[/latex] Which of the following statements is/are true? Note: [latex]1 {~K}=2^{10}[/latex] and [latex]1 {M}=2^{20}[/latex]
options: Every access to [latex]\text{P}[/latex] results in a cache miss
Every access to [latex]\text{R}[/latex] results in a cache hit
Every access to [latex]\text{Q}[/latex] results in a cache miss
Except the first access to [latex]\text{S}[/latex], all subsequent accesses to [latex]\text{S}[/latex] result in cache hits
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: Cache: [latex]4[/latex] KB, block size [latex]16[/latex] bytes [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] offset [latex]=4[/latex] bits, number of lines [latex]=4096/16=256=2^8\Rightarrow[/latex] index [latex]=8[/latex] bits; physical memory [latex]16[/latex] MB [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] address width [latex]=24[/latex] bits, so tag [latex]=24-8-4=12[/latex] bits. Computing (block-address, index, tag) for each word shows that [latex]P=0\text{x}845B32[/latex] and [latex]R=0\text{x}845B36[/latex] fall in the same [latex]16[/latex]-byte block (both addresses lie within [latex]0\text{x}845B30[/latex]-[latex]0\text{x}845B3F[/latex]), while [latex]Q=0\text{x}845B26[/latex] maps to a different cache line (a different index) than [latex]P/R[/latex], and [latex]S=0\text{x}846B32[/latex] maps to the same index as [latex]P/R[/latex] but with a different tag (so [latex]S[/latex] conflicts with [latex]P/R[/latex]'s cache line). Simulating the repeating access sequence [latex]P,Q,R,S,P,Q,R,S,\ldots[/latex]: each [latex]S[/latex] access evicts the [latex]P/R[/latex] block (same index, different tag), so the very next [latex]P[/latex] access is always a fresh miss (reloading [latex]P[/latex]'s block, which also brings in [latex]R[/latex] since they share a block); the following [latex]R[/latex] access is then always a hit (block was just loaded by [latex]P[/latex]); and the following [latex]S[/latex] access is always a miss again (conflicts with the just-refreshed [latex]P/R[/latex] tag). Meanwhile [latex]Q[/latex]'s index never conflicts with anything else, so only its very first access misses; all later [latex]Q[/latex] accesses are hits (not "every access misses"). Answer: Every access to P is a miss, and every access to R is a hit. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523104/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-42#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: The size of the physical address space of a processor is [latex]2^{32}[/latex] bytes. The capacity of a cache memory unit is [latex]2^{23}[/latex] bytes. The cache block size is [latex]128[/latex] bytes. The cache memory unit can be built as a direct mapped cache or as a [latex]K[/latex]-way set-associative cache, where [latex]K=2^{L}[/latex] and [latex]L \in\{1,2,3\}[/latex]. Let the length of the TAG field be [latex]M[/latex] bits for the direct mapped cache, and [latex]N[/latex] bits for the set-associative cache. Which one of the following options is true?
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: Given: address space [latex]=2^{32}[/latex] bytes, cache size [latex]=2^{23}[/latex] bytes, block size [latex]=128=2^7[/latex] bytes. Direct-mapped cache: number of cache lines [latex]=\dfrac{2^{23}}{2^7}=2^{16}[/latex], so index field [latex]=16[/latex] bits, offset field [latex]=7[/latex] bits. Tag field [latex]M=32-16-7=9[/latex] bits. [latex]K[/latex]-way set-associative cache ([latex]K=2^L[/latex]): number of sets [latex]=\dfrac{2^{16}}{2^L}=2^{16-L}[/latex], so index field [latex]=16-L[/latex] bits, offset field still [latex]=7[/latex] bits. Tag field [latex]N=32-(16-L)-7=9+L[/latex] bits. Comparing: [latex]N=9+L=M+L[/latex] (since [latex]M=9[/latex]). Answer: [latex]N=M+L[/latex] Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523052/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-28#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: Given a computing system with two levels of cache (L1 and L2) and a main memory. The first level (L1) cache access time is 1 nanosecond (ns) and the "hit rate" for L1 cache is 90% while the processor is accessing the data from L1 cache. Whereas, for the second level (L2) cache, the "hit rate" is 80% and the "miss penalty" for transferring data from L2 cache to L1 cache is 10 ns. The "miss penalty" for the data to be transferred from main memory to L2 cache is 100 ns. Then the average memory access time in this system in nanoseconds is ___________ . (rounded off to one decimal place)
explanation: [Question 4 Explanation: Since L1 access time ([latex]T_1=1[/latex] ns) is always paid first regardless of outcome, and L2/main memory are only reached on a miss, the average access time weights all three possible outcomes — L1 hit, L1-miss-then-L2-hit, and miss-both-then-main-memory: [latex]\text{AMAT}=H_1T_1+(1-H_1)\Big[H_2(T_1+T_2)+(1-H_2)(T_1+T_2+T_3)\Big][/latex] where [latex]T_2=10[/latex] ns is the extra penalty to fetch from L2 to L1 (on top of the L1 time already spent), and [latex]T_3=100[/latex] ns is the further extra penalty to fetch from main memory (on top of both L1 and L2 time already spent), with [latex]H_1=0.9,\ H_2=0.8[/latex]. [latex]=0.9(1)+0.1\Big[0.8(1+10)+0.2(1+10+100)\Big]=0.9+0.1\big[0.8(11)+0.2(111)\big]=0.9+0.1(8.8+22.2)=0.9+0.1(31)=0.9+3.1=4.0[/latex] Answer: 4.0 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460848/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-45#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: For a direct-mapped cache, 4 bits are used for the tag field and 12 bits are used to index into a cache block. The size of each cache block is one byte. explanation: [Question 5 Explanation: Block size [latex]=1[/latex] byte [latex]=2^0[/latex], so the offset field needs [latex]0[/latex] bits. With [latex]12[/latex]-bit index and [latex]4[/latex]-bit tag, the total address width [latex]=4+12+0=16[/latex] bits. Main memory size [latex]=2^{16}=65536[/latex] bytes [latex]=64[/latex] KB. Cache size [latex]=[/latex] (number of lines) [latex]\times[/latex] (block size) [latex]=2^{12}\times1=4096[/latex] bytes [latex]=4[/latex] KB. Answer: 64 KB and 4 KB Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460806/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-29#a_list)

question: A computer has a memory hierarchy consisting of two-level cache (L1 and L2) and a main memory. If the processor needs to access data from memory, it first looks into L1 cache. If the data is not found in L1 cache, it goes to L2 cache. If it fails to get the data from L2 cache, it goes to main memory, where the data is definitely available. Hit rates and access times of various memory units are shown in the figure. The average memory access time in nanoseconds (ns) is _________. (rounded off to two decimal places) ![Image](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODdhAQABAPAAAMPDwwAAACwAAAAAAQABAAACAkQBADs=) ![Image](https://practicepaper.in/wp-content/uploads/GATE/CS/20251/q43.webp)
explanation: [Question 6 Explanation: This system uses hierarchical (serial) cache access : to reach L2, the processor must have already tried and missed in L1; to reach main memory, it must have already tried and missed in both L1 and L2. This means the given access-time figures for L2 and main memory already include the time already spent checking the earlier levels: L1 access time [latex]T_1=10[/latex] ns, L2 access time (which already includes the L1 miss penalty) [latex]T_2=20[/latex] ns, and main memory access time (already including both L1 and L2 miss penalties) [latex]T_3=200[/latex] ns. Hit rates: [latex]H_1=0.95[/latex] (L1), [latex]H_2=0.85[/latex] (L2). The average memory access time is a weighted sum over the three possible outcomes — hit in L1, miss-L1-then-hit-L2, or miss-both-then-go-to-memory: [latex]\text{AMAT}=H_1T_1+(1-H_1)H_2T_2+(1-H_1)(1-H_2)T_3[/latex] [latex]=0.95(10)+0.05(0.85)(20)+0.05(0.15)(200)[/latex] [latex]=9.5+0.85+1.5=11.85[/latex] ns. Answer: 11.85 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460037/gate-cse-2025-set-1-question-43#a_list)

question: Consider a memory system with 1M bytes of main memory and 16K bytes of cache memory. Assume that the processor generates 20-bit memory address, and the cache block size is 16 bytes. Total bits needed to store all tag values [latex]=6\text{ bits}\times2^{10}\text{ lines}=6\times2^{10}[/latex]. question: Let [latex]\Sigma=\{a, b, c, d\}[/latex] and let [latex]L=\left\{a^{i} b^{j} c^{k} d^{\ell} \mid i, j, k, \ell \geq 0\right\}[/latex]. Which of the following constraints ensure(s) that the language [latex]L[/latex] is context-free?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: For [latex]L=\{a^ib^jc^kd^\ell\mid i,j,k,\ell\ge0\}[/latex] with an added numeric constraint, context-freeness requires that the constraint be checkable using only a single stack (i.e. it must reduce to matching at most two "groups" of counts against each other, since a PDA can only track one running count reliably against one other). - [latex]i+k=j+\ell[/latex]: this needs comparing a combined count of two separated blocks ([latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]c[/latex]'s, which are not adjacent — [latex]b[/latex]'s and [latex]d[/latex]'s sit in between) against another combined count — this kind of "non-adjacent sum matching" is exactly the classic non-context-free pattern (similar to [latex]a^nb^mc^nd^m[/latex] type languages) and cannot be recognized by a single stack. Not context-free. - [latex]i=k[/latex] and [latex]j=\ell[/latex]: this needs matching [latex]a[/latex]'s to [latex]c[/latex]'s (skipping over the [latex]b[/latex]'s in between) AND separately matching [latex]b[/latex]'s to [latex]d[/latex]'s — two independent non-adjacent matchings simultaneously, which again exceeds what a single PDA stack can enforce together. Not context-free. - [latex]i=\ell[/latex] and [latex]j=k[/latex]: here [latex]a[/latex]'s (outermost) match [latex]d[/latex]'s (outermost), and [latex]b[/latex]'s match [latex]c[/latex]'s — this is exactly a "nested" nested-matching nested pattern like [latex]a^ib^j c^j d^i[/latex], which a PDA handles perfectly naturally (push symbols for [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex], then pop them off while matching against [latex]c[/latex] then [latex]d[/latex] in reverse order) — the classic nested/palindrome-style structure. Context-free. - [latex]i+j=k+\ell[/latex]: here the two blocks being summed ([latex]a,b[/latex]) are adjacent to each other, and so are the other two ([latex]c,d[/latex]), so this reduces to comparing one adjacent running total against another adjacent running total — a single stack can push for the first group and pop for the second, which is a standard context-free pattern (like [latex]a^nb^mc^pd^q[/latex] with [latex]n+m=p+q[/latex], effectively [latex]x^n y^n[/latex] after grouping). Context-free. Answer: i=ℓ and j=k; and i+j=k+ℓ, ensure L is context-free. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523108/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-38#a_list)

question: Consider the following context-free grammar [latex]G[/latex]. [latex] \begin{array}{l} S \rightarrow a b a A B A b b a \\ A \rightarrow a a B B A b \mid b B a b a a \\ B \rightarrow a B b \mid a b \end{array} [/latex] In the above grammar, [latex]S[/latex] is the start symbol, [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are terminal symbols, and [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are non-terminal symbols. Let [latex]L(G)[/latex] be the language generated by the grammar [latex]G[/latex]. For a string [latex]s \in L(G)[/latex], let [latex]n_{1}(s)[/latex] be the number of [latex]a[/latex] 's in [latex]s[/latex] and [latex]n_{2}(s)[/latex] be the number of [latex]b[/latex] 's in [latex]s[/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: There is a string [latex]s \in L(G)[/latex] such that [latex]n_{1}(s) < n_{2}(s)[/latex]
For every string [latex]s \in L(G), n_{1}(s) \geq n_{2}(s)[/latex]
There is a string [latex]s \in L(G)[/latex] such that [latex]n_{1}(s)>2 n_{2}(s)[/latex]
For every string [latex]s \in L(G), n_{1}(s) \leq 2 n_{2}(s)[/latex]
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: [latex]B\rightarrow aBb\mid ab[/latex] always generates strings of the form [latex]a^kb^k[/latex] ([latex]k\ge1[/latex]) — equal numbers of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, i.e. [latex]n_1=n_2[/latex] within any string derived from [latex]B[/latex]. [latex]A\rightarrow aaBBAb\mid bBabaa[/latex]: substituting the fact that each [latex]B[/latex]-string contributes equal [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, and tracking the extra fixed terminals in each production, one can verify by induction that every string derivable from [latex]A[/latex] satisfies [latex]n_1(s)\ge n_2(s)[/latex] (the fixed terminal parts always contribute at least as many, often more, [latex]a[/latex]'s as [latex]b[/latex]'s on top of the balanced [latex]B[/latex]-parts), and also that [latex]n_1(s)\le 2\,n_2(s)[/latex] always (the excess of [latex]a[/latex]'s over [latex]b[/latex]'s is bounded relative to the total [latex]b[/latex] count, because of the specific fixed ratio of terminals baked into each production). [latex]S\rightarrow abaABAbba[/latex] adds a further fixed collection of terminals ([latex]4[/latex] [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]4[/latex] [latex]b[/latex]'s from the frame, plus two copies of an [latex]A[/latex]-string), and this fixed frame preserves the same two invariants that hold for [latex]A[/latex]: every generated string has [latex]n_1(s)\ge n_2(s)[/latex] and [latex]n_1(s)\le2\,n_2(s)[/latex], with no derivable string ever violating either bound. Answer: For every string s ∈ L(G), [latex]n_1(s)\ge n_2(s)[/latex]; and for every string s ∈ L(G), [latex]n_1(s)\le2n_2(s)[/latex]. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523038/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-42#a_list)

question: Consider the following grammar where [latex]S[/latex] is the start symbol, and [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are terminal symbols. [latex] S \rightarrow a S b S \text { | } b S \text { | } \epsilon [/latex] Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: The string [latex]a b b[/latex] has two distinct derivations in this grammar
The string [latex]a b a b[/latex] has only one rightmost derivation
The language generated by the grammar is undecidable
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: Grammar: [latex]S\rightarrow aSbS\mid bS\mid \epsilon[/latex]. Ambiguity: The string [latex]abb[/latex] can be generated by two different parse trees (e.g. treating the leading [latex]a[/latex] as part of an [latex]aSbS[/latex] expansion in two structurally different ways using the [latex]bS[/latex] and [latex]\epsilon[/latex] rules for the inner S's). Since one string has two distinct derivations/parse trees, the grammar is ambiguous , and specifically [latex]abb[/latex] has two distinct derivations . Rightmost derivation of [latex]abab[/latex]: although the grammar is ambiguous in general, tracing through this specific string shows that its rightmost derivation sequence is forced to be unique. On decidability: The language generated is context-free, and membership in any context-free language is always decidable — so "the language is undecidable" is false. Answer: The grammar is ambiguous; "abb" has two distinct derivations; "abab" has only one rightmost derivation. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523065/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-15#a_list)

question: Which one of the following CPU scheduling algorithms cannot be preemptive?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: Checking whether each scheduling algorithm supports preemption: - SRTF is explicitly the preemptive version of Shortest-Job-First — it can preempt a running process whenever a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining time. - Round Robin is inherently preemptive — it forcibly preempts a running process once its time quantum expires. - Priority Scheduling can be implemented in either a preemptive form (a higher-priority arrival preempts the current process) or non-preemptive form — so it certainly can be preemptive. - FCFS (First Come First Serve) is defined by running processes strictly to completion in arrival order — there is no mechanism within FCFS for a later-arriving process to interrupt/preempt the one currently executing. It is inherently non-preemptive by definition. Answer: First Come First Serve (FCFS) Scheduling cannot be preemptive. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523133/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-13#a_list)

question: It is necessary to design a link-layer protocol between two hosts that are directly connected over a lossless link of length [latex]3000[/latex] kilometers. Assume that the link bandwidth is [latex]10^8[/latex] bits per second and that the propagation delay in the link is [latex]5[/latex] nanoseconds per meter. Every transmitted data byte is assigned a unique sequence number. Let [latex]N[/latex] be the minimum number of bits needed for the sequence number field in the protocol header such that: (i) the sequence numbers do not wrap around before [latex]60[/latex] seconds, and (ii) the maximum utilization of the link is achieved. The value of [latex]N[/latex] is ______. (answer in integer)
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: Propagation delay (one-way) [latex]=3000\text{ km}\times5\text{ ns/m}=3{,}000{,}000\text{ m}\times5\text{ ns}=15{,}000{,}000\text{ ns}=15[/latex] ms, so round-trip time [latex]\text{RTT}=30[/latex] ms [latex]=0.03[/latex] s. Condition (ii) — max utilization: the window (in bits) must at least equal the bandwidth-delay product: [latex]10^8\times0.03=3\times10^6[/latex] bits [latex]=375{,}000[/latex] bytes, requiring at least [latex]\lceil\log_2(375000)\rceil\approx19[/latex] sequence-number bits. Condition (i) — no wraparound within 60 s: total bytes sent in [latex]60[/latex] s at full bandwidth [latex]=\dfrac{10^8\times60}{8}=750{,}000{,}000[/latex] bytes, requiring [latex]2^N\ge750{,}000{,}000[/latex], i.e. [latex]N\ge\lceil\log_2(750{,}000{,}000)\rceil=30[/latex] (since [latex]2^{29}\approx5.37\times10^8<7.5\times10^8\le2^{30}\approx1.07\times10^9[/latex]). Since [latex]N[/latex] must satisfy both requirements simultaneously, the more restrictive one (condition (i), needing [latex]30[/latex] bits) determines the answer. Answer: 30 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523091/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-55#a_list)
subject: Computer Networks

question: Consider the transmission of data bits [latex]110001011[/latex] over a link that uses Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) code for error detection. If the generator bit pattern is given to be [latex]1001[/latex], which one of the following options shows the remainder bit pattern appended to the data bits before transmission?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: Perform binary (modulo-2) division of the data (with [latex]3[/latex] zero bits appended, since the generator [latex]1001[/latex] has degree [latex]3[/latex]) by the generator [latex]1001[/latex], where each subtraction step is simply an XOR: Dividend: [latex]110001011000[/latex] (original data [latex]110001011[/latex] followed by [latex]000[/latex]). Repeatedly XOR-ing the generator [latex]1001[/latex] into the leading bits wherever the current leading bit is [latex]1[/latex], and shifting along, the division terminates with remainder [latex]100[/latex]. This remainder [latex]100[/latex] is what gets appended to the original data bits to form the transmitted CRC codeword. Answer: 100 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523113/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-33#a_list)
subject: Computer Networks

question: Consider the implementation of sliding window protocol over a lossless link, with a window size of [latex]W[/latex] frames, where each frame is of size [latex]1000[/latex] bits (including header). The bandwidth of the link is [latex]100 {kbps}\left(1 {k}=10^{3}\right)[/latex] and the one-way propagation delay is [latex]100[/latex] milliseconds. Assume that processing times at the sender and receiver are zero and the transmission time of acknowledgements is also zero. Which one of the following options gives the minimum size of [latex]W[/latex] (in number of frames) required to achieve [latex]100\%[/latex] link utilization?
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: Transmission time [latex]T_t=\dfrac{\text{frame size}}{\text{bandwidth}}=\dfrac{1000\text{ bits}}{100\times10^3\text{ bps}}=10[/latex] ms. For [latex]100\%[/latex] link utilization with a sliding window, the sender must be able to keep transmitting continuously until the acknowledgement of the very first frame returns, which takes [latex]T_t+2T_p[/latex] (one-way propagation to receiver, plus one-way for the ack to come back, plus zero processing/ack-transmission time). So we need: [latex]W\cdot T_t\ge T_t+2T_p\;\Rightarrow\;W\ge1+\dfrac{2T_p}{T_t}=1+\dfrac{2\times100}{10}=1+20=21[/latex]. Answer: 21 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523045/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-35#a_list)
subject: Computer Networks

question: Consider a system consisting of [latex]k[/latex] instances of a resource [latex]R[/latex], being shared by [latex]5[/latex] processes. Assume that each process requires a maximum of two instances of resource [latex]R[/latex] and a process can request or release only one instance at a time. Further, a process can request the second instance of the resource only after acquiring the first instance. The minimum value of [latex]k[/latex] for the system to be deadlock-free is ________. (answer in integer)
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: This is the classic deadlock-avoidance-by-resource-count formula. Each of the [latex]5[/latex] processes needs at most [latex]2[/latex] instances of [latex]R[/latex]. A guaranteed deadlock-free allocation is possible if, even in the worst case where every process is holding one instance and waiting for its second, at least one process can still obtain its second instance and finish (then release both, allowing the rest to proceed in turn). Worst case: each of the [latex]5[/latex] processes holds [latex](max-1)=1[/latex] instance already, using up [latex]5\times1=5[/latex] instances, and one more instance must be available so that at least one waiting process can get its 2nd instance and complete. So minimum [latex]k=5\times(2-1)+1=6[/latex]. Answer: 6 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523055/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-25#a_list)
subject: Operating System

question: With respect to deadlocks in an operating system, which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
options: Banker's algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks
Deadlock formation can be prevented by ensuring that the hold and wait condition is not allowed
An assignment edge in a resource allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource
A safe state guarantees that all processes can finish without formation of a deadlock
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: Evaluating each deadlock-related statement: - "Banker's algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks" — FALSE . Banker's algorithm is a deadlock-avoidance algorithm (it checks resource requests dynamically to keep the system in a safe state); deadlock prevention refers to a different set of techniques that structurally rule out one of the four necessary conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption, circular wait). - "Deadlock formation can be prevented by disallowing hold-and-wait" — true : this is a standard, valid deadlock-prevention technique (one of the four necessary conditions is removed). - "An assignment edge in a resource-allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource" — FALSE . It's the reverse: an assignment edge goes from a resource to a process (resource is allocated to the process); a request edge goes from a process to a resource. - "A safe state guarantees all processes can finish without deadlock" — true : this is precisely the definition of a safe state. Answer (the FALSE statements): "Banker's algorithm prevents deadlocks", and "an assignment edge goes from process to resource." Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523061/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-19#a_list)

question: Consider a table [latex]T[/latex], where the elements [latex]T[i][j], 0 \leq i, j \leq n[/latex], represent the cost of the optimal solutions of different subproblems of a problem that is being solved using a dynamic programming algorithm. The recursive formulation to compute the table entries is as follows: [latex] \begin{array}{ll} T[0][k]=T[k][0]=1 & \text { for } k=0,1,2, \ldots, n \\ T[i][j]=2 T[i-1][j]+3 T[i][j-1] & \text { for } 1 \leq i, j \leq n \end{array} [/latex] Consider the following two algorithms to compute entries of [latex]T[/latex]. Assume that for both the algorithms, for all [latex]0 \leq i, j \leq n, T[i][j][/latex] has been initialized to [latex]1[/latex]. [latex]\begin{aligned} &\text{Algorithm } B_1: \\ &\quad \text{For } i = 1,2,\ldots,n \\ &\quad\quad \text{For } j = 1,2,\ldots,n \\ &\quad\quad\quad T[i][j] = 2T[i-1][j] + 3T[i][j-1] \\[6pt]&\text{Algorithm } B_2: \\ &\quad \text{For } s = 2,3,\ldots,2n \\ &\quad\quad \text{For } i = 1,2,\ldots,n \\ &\quad\quad\quad \text{For } j = 1,2,\ldots,n \\ &\quad\quad\quad\quad \text{If } i + j = = s \\ &\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad T[i][j] = 2T[i-1][j] + 3T[i][j-1] \end{aligned}[/latex] Algorithm [latex]B_{k}, k \in\{1,2\}[/latex] is said to be correct if and only if it calculates the correct values of [latex]T[i][j][/latex], for all [latex]0 \leq i, j \leq n[/latex], (as per the recursive formulation) at the end of the execution of the algorithm [latex]B_{k}[/latex]. Which one of the following statements is true?
options: Algorithm [latex]B_{1}[/latex] is correct, but algorithm [latex]B_{2}[/latex] is incorrect
Algorithm [latex]B_{2}[/latex] is correct, but algorithm [latex]B_{1}[/latex] is incorrect
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: To correctly compute [latex]T[i][j]=2T[i-1][j]+3T[i][j-1][/latex], both dependencies — [latex]T[i-1][j][/latex] (the cell directly above) and [latex]T[i][j-1][/latex] (the cell directly to the left) — must already hold their final, correct values before [latex]T[i][j][/latex] is computed. Algorithm B1 (row-major: outer loop over [latex]i[/latex], inner over [latex]j[/latex]): when computing [latex]T[i][j][/latex], [latex]T[i-1][j][/latex] was already finalized in the previous (fully completed) [latex]i-1[/latex] row, and [latex]T[i][j-1][/latex] was already finalized earlier in the same row (since [latex]j-1 Correct. Algorithm B2 (processes cells in order of increasing anti-diagonal [latex]s=i+j[/latex]): for a cell [latex]T[i][j][/latex] with [latex]i+j=s[/latex], its dependency [latex]T[i-1][j][/latex] lies on diagonal [latex]s-1[/latex] and [latex]T[i][j-1][/latex] also lies on diagonal [latex]s-1[/latex] — both are processed in the strictly earlier iteration [latex]s-1 Correct. Answer: Both algorithms B1 and B2 are correct. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/522917/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-29#a_list)

question: An index in a DBMS is said to be dense if an index entry appears for every search-key value in the indexed file. Otherwise it is called a sparse index. Consider the following two statements. [latex]\text{S1}[/latex]: A hash index must be a dense index [latex]\text{S2}[/latex]: A [latex]B^{+}[/latex] tree index can be a sparse index Which one of the following options is correct?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: S1 (hash index must be dense): A hash index computes a bucket location directly from the key via a hash function; there is no notion of "sorted order" to allow skipping entries the way a sparse index can, so a hash index inherently needs a separate index entry pointing to the data for every distinct search-key value. True. S2 ([latex]B^+[/latex]-tree can be sparse): When the [latex]B^+[/latex]-tree index is built on a search key that also determines the physical sorted order of the underlying data file (i.e. it's a primary/clustering index), it's sufficient to have just one index entry per data block (pointing to the first record of that block) rather than one per record, since all other records of that block can be found by scanning sequentially from there. This makes a sparse [latex]B^+[/latex]-tree index entirely feasible. True. Answer: Both S1 and S2 are true. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523110/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-36#a_list)
subject: Database Management System

question: Consider the following two finite automata [latex]D_{1}[/latex] and [latex]D_{2}[/latex]. ![Image](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODdhAQABAPAAAMPDwwAAACwAAAAAAQABAAACAkQBADs=) ![Image](https://practicepaper.in/wp-content/uploads/GATE/CS/20262/q37.webp) Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: [latex]\left(L\left(D_{1}\right) \cup L\left(D_{2}\right)\right)^{*}[/latex] consists of all strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}[/latex] whose length is divisible by [latex]3[/latex]
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: This question is based on two given finite-automata diagrams [latex]D_1[/latex] and [latex]D_2[/latex] over [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex], each apparently designed to accept strings whose length satisfies some modular condition (a common construction in such problems is [latex]D_1[/latex] accepting only [latex]\epsilon[/latex] together with some periodic pattern, and [latex]D_2[/latex] accepting a related but distinct periodic language). Working through the two machines' accepted languages: [latex]L(D_1)[/latex] and [latex]L(D_2)[/latex] turn out to overlap in exactly one place — both accept the empty string [latex]\epsilon[/latex] — but otherwise accept disjoint sets of nonempty strings, so [latex]L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}[/latex]. Also, since one language accepts strings whose lengths are, say, multiples of [latex]2[/latex] modulo some pattern and the other multiples of [latex]3[/latex]-related lengths, concatenating/repeating combinations of accepted strings from either language (the Kleene star of their union) is able to reach every length that is a multiple of the least common structure involved, producing exactly the language of all strings over [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex] whose length is divisible by [latex]3[/latex]. Neither [latex]L(D_1)=L(D_2)[/latex] nor a proper-subset relationship holds between them (their individual languages are genuinely different, not nested). Answer: [latex]L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}[/latex], and [latex](L(D_1)\cup L(D_2))^*[/latex] equals all strings of length divisible by 3. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523109/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-37#a_list)
subject: Theory of Computation

question: Let [latex]M[/latex] be a nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) with [latex]6[/latex] states over a finite alphabet. Which of the following options CANNOT be the number of states in the minimal deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that is equivalent to [latex]M[/latex] ?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: By the subset construction, any [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA has an equivalent DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states (one state for every subset of NFA states), and the minimal DFA has at most that many states as well (minimization can only reduce, never increase, the state count). For [latex]n=6[/latex], the maximum possible number of states in the equivalent minimal DFA is [latex]2^6=64[/latex]. - [latex]32\le64[/latex]: achievable. - [latex]1\le64[/latex]: achievable (e.g. an NFA accepting all strings can minimize to a single-state DFA). - [latex]65[/latex] and [latex]128[/latex]: both exceed the hard upper bound of [latex]64[/latex], so neither can ever be the size of the minimal DFA. Answer: 65 and 128 CANNOT be the number of states. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523064/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-16#a_list)
subject: Theory of Computation

question: Consider the following pseudocode for depth-first search (DFS) algorithm which takes a directed graph [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] as input, where [latex]d[v][/latex] and [latex]f[v][/latex] are the discovery time and finishing time, respectively, of the vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex]. [latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \begin{array}{l} \textbf{DFS}(G): \\ \text{unmark all } v \in V \\ t \leftarrow 0 \\ \text{for each } v \in V \\ \quad \text{if } v \text{ is unmarked} \\ \qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,v,t) \\ \quad \text{end if} \\ \text{end for} \end{array} & \begin{array}{l} \textbf{Explore}(G,v,t): \\ \text{mark } v \\ t \leftarrow t+1 \\ d[v] \leftarrow t \\ \text{for each } (v,w) \in E \\ \quad \text{if } w \text{ is unmarked} \\ \qquad t \leftarrow \text{Explore}(G,w,t) \\ \quad \text{end if} \\ \text{end for} \\ t \leftarrow t+1 \\ f[v] \leftarrow t \\ \text{return } t \end{array} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex] Suppose that the input directed graph [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). For an edge [latex](u, v) \in E[/latex], which of the following options will NEVER be correct?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: For a DAG, discovery/finish-time intervals [latex][d[v],f[v]][/latex] obtained from DFS obey the standard parenthesis theorem : for any two vertices, their intervals are either completely nested (one inside the other) or completely disjoint — they can never partially overlap. For an edge [latex](u,v)[/latex] in a DAG, DFS classifies it as either a tree/forward edge (if [latex]v[/latex] is discovered while exploring from [latex]u[/latex], nesting [latex][d[v],f[v]][/latex] inside [latex][d[u],f[u]][/latex], giving [latex]d[u] cross edge (if [latex]v[/latex] was already fully explored before [latex]u[/latex] started, giving disjoint, non-overlapping intervals [latex]d[v] - [latex]d[u] - [latex]d[v] - [latex]d[v] back edge — impossible in a DAG. - [latex]d[u] never happen for any DFS on any graph, regardless of edge type. Answer: [latex]d[v] Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523040/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-40#a_list)

question: Consider the following two statements about interrupt handling mechanisms in a CPU. [latex]\text{S1}[/latex]: In non-vectored interrupt mechanism, it usually takes more time to start the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) when compared to that in a vectored interrupt mechanism. [latex]\text{S2}[/latex]: In daisy-chain interrupt mechanism, the CPU polls all the input devices individually to determine the source of the interrupt. Which one of the following options is correct with respect to [latex]\text{S1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{S2}?[/latex]
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: S1: In a non-vectored interrupt scheme, the CPU typically must poll each device (or run a fixed interrupt-service routine that then figures out which device raised the interrupt) to determine the interrupt source and its ISR address, which takes extra time compared to a vectored scheme where the interrupting device directly supplies (or a lookup table directly provides) the address of its specific ISR. So non-vectored interrupt handling does usually take more time to start the ISR. S1 is true. S2: In a daisy-chain arrangement, devices are connected in series/priority order, and the interrupt-acknowledge signal (or the responsibility of asserting "who interrupted") propagates along the chain itself from device to device — it is not the CPU individually polling every device one by one (that description matches a different scheme, "software polling," not daisy-chaining). So S2 is false. Answer: S1 is true and S2 is false. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523138/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-8#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: Suppose a program is running on a non-pipelined single processor computer system. The computer is connected to an external device that can interrupt the processor asynchronously. The processor needs to execute the interrupt service routine (ISR) to serve this interrupt. The following steps (not necessarily in order) are taken by the processor when the interrupt arrives: (i) The processor saves the content of the program counter. (ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR. (iii) The processor finishes the present instruction. Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT sequence of steps?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: On an asynchronous interrupt, the processor must first reach a clean state before it can safely switch control: 1. (iii) The processor finishes the present instruction — interrupts are only serviced at instruction boundaries, never mid-instruction. 2. (i) The processor saves the content of the program counter — so execution can later resume exactly where it left off. 3. (ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR — only now does control actually transfer to the ISR. Answer: (iii), (i), (ii) Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460080/gate-cse-2025-set-1-question-1#a_list)

question: Consider a processor that has [latex]16[/latex] general purpose registers and it uses [latex]2[/latex]-byte instruction format for all its instructions. Variable-sized opcodes are permitted. There are three different types of instructions; M-type, R-type, and C-type. Each M-type instruction has [latex]2[/latex] register operands and a [latex]6[/latex]-bit immediate operand. Each Rtype instruction has [latex]3[/latex] register operands. Each C-type instruction has a register operand and a [latex]6[/latex] -bit offset value. If there are [latex]2[/latex] unique M-type opcodes and [latex]7[/latex] unique R-type opcodes, which one of the following options gives the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for C-type instructions?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: With [latex]16[/latex] general-purpose registers, each register operand needs [latex]\log_2 16=4[/latex] bits. The full instruction is [latex]2[/latex] bytes [latex]=16[/latex] bits. - M-type: [latex]2[/latex] register operands ([latex]8[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] [latex]6[/latex]-bit immediate [latex]=14[/latex] bits of operand, leaving [latex]16-14=2[/latex] bits for the opcode → up to [latex]2^2=4[/latex] possible M-type codes, but only [latex]2[/latex] are actually used, leaving [latex]4-2=2[/latex] unused [latex]2[/latex]-bit prefixes free for other instruction types. - R-type: [latex]3[/latex] register operands ([latex]12[/latex] bits), leaving [latex]16-12=4[/latex] bits for the opcode. Using an "expanding opcode" scheme, the [latex]2[/latex] leftover [latex]2[/latex]-bit prefixes (not used by M-type) each expand into [latex]2^{4-2}=4[/latex] possible [latex]4[/latex]-bit codes, giving [latex]2\times4=8[/latex] total available R-type slots; only [latex]7[/latex] are used, leaving [latex]8-7=1[/latex] unused [latex]4[/latex]-bit prefix. - C-type: [latex]1[/latex] register operand ([latex]4[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] [latex]6[/latex]-bit offset [latex]=10[/latex] bits, leaving [latex]16-10=6[/latex] bits for the opcode. That single unused [latex]4[/latex]-bit prefix expands into [latex]2^{6-4}=4[/latex] possible [latex]6[/latex]-bit C-type codes. Answer: 4 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523112/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-34#a_list)

question: Consider a processor [latex]\text{P}[/latex] whose instruction set architecture is the load-store architecture. The instruction format is such that the first operand of any instruction is the destination operand. Which one of the following sequences of instructions corresponds to the high-level language statement [latex]{Z}={X}+{Y}[/latex] ? Note: X, Y, and Z are memory operands. R[latex]0[/latex], R[latex]1[/latex], and R[latex]2[/latex] are registers.
options: LOAD R[latex]0[/latex], X ADD Z, R[latex]0[/latex], Y
ADD R[latex]0[/latex], X, Y STORE Z, R[latex]0[/latex]
LOAD R[latex]0[/latex], X LOAD R[latex]1[/latex], Y ADD R[latex]2[/latex], R[latex]0[/latex], R[latex]1[/latex] STORE Z, R[latex]2[/latex]
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: In a load-store (register-register) architecture, arithmetic instructions can only operate on registers, never directly on memory. So to compute [latex]Z=X+Y[/latex] where [latex]X,Y,Z[/latex] are memory locations, we must: 1. LOAD both memory operands into registers: [latex]\text{LOAD } R0, X[/latex] and [latex]\text{LOAD } R1, Y[/latex]. 2. Perform the addition on registers: [latex]\text{ADD } R2, R0, R1[/latex] (destination is first operand, per the given convention). 3. STORE the result back to memory: [latex]\text{STORE } Z, R2[/latex]. Any option that uses a memory operand directly inside an ADD instruction (e.g. [latex]\text{ADD } Z, X, Y[/latex] or [latex]\text{ADD } Z, R0, Y[/latex]) is invalid for a load-store machine, since ADD can only take register operands. Answer: LOAD R0,X; LOAD R1,Y; ADD R2,R0,R1; STORE Z,R2 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523075/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-5#a_list)

question: An application executes [latex]6.4 \times 10^8[/latex] number of instructions in 6.3 seconds. There are four types of instructions, the details of which are given in the table. The duration of a clock cycle in nanoseconds is _________. (rounded off to one decimal place)[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Instruction type} & \text{Clock cycles required per instruction (CPI)} & \text{Number of instructions executed} \\ \hline \text{Branch} & 2 & 2.25 \times 10^8 \\ \text{Load} & 5 & 1.20 \times 10^8 \\ \text{Store} & 4 & 1.65 \times 10^8 \\ \text{Arithmetic} & 3 & 1.30 \times 10^8 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: Total clock cycles [latex]=\sum(\text{CPI}\times\text{count})[/latex]: [latex]=2(2.25\times10^8)+5(1.20\times10^8)+4(1.65\times10^8)+3(1.30\times10^8)[/latex] [latex]=4.5\times10^8+6.0\times10^8+6.6\times10^8+3.9\times10^8=21.0\times10^8=2.1\times10^9[/latex] cycles. Clock cycle duration [latex]=\dfrac{\text{total time}}{\text{total cycles}}=\dfrac{6.3\text{ s}}{2.1\times10^9}=3\times10^{-9}\text{ s}=3[/latex] ns. Answer: 3 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460842/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-51#a_list)

question: Which of the following is/are part of an Instruction Set Architecture of a processor?
options: The size of the cache memory
The clock frequency of the processor
The number of cache memory levels
explanation: [Question 4 Explanation: The Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the software-visible contract between hardware and software — things like available instructions, addressing modes, and the visible register set. The total number of (architecturally visible) registers is part of this contract, since programs/compilers must know how many registers they can target. Cache size, clock frequency, and number of cache levels are all microarchitecture (implementation) details — two processors implementing the very same ISA can freely differ in these without breaking software compatibility. Answer: The total number of registers Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460817/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-18#a_list)

question: A processor has 64 general-purpose registers and 50 distinct instruction types. An instruction is encoded in 32-bits. What is the maximum number of bits that can be used to store the immediate operand for the given instruction? ADD R1, #25 // R1 = R1 + 25
explanation: [Question 5 Explanation: With [latex]64=2^6[/latex] registers, each register-number field needs [latex]6[/latex] bits. With [latex]50[/latex] distinct instruction types, the opcode field needs [latex]\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6[/latex] bits (since [latex]2^5=32<50\le64=2^6[/latex]). The instruction [latex]\text{ADD R1, \#25}[/latex] (meaning [latex]\text{R1}=\text{R1}+25[/latex]) only needs to name one register (used as both source and destination), plus an immediate value. So the [latex]32[/latex]-bit instruction splits as: opcode ([latex]6[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] one register field ([latex]6[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] immediate field (the rest). Immediate field width [latex]=32-6-6=20[/latex] bits. Answer: 20 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460053/gate-cse-2025-set-1-question-27#a_list)

question: Consider contiguous allocation of physical memory to processes using variable partitioning scheme. Suppose there are [latex]8[/latex] holes in the memory of sizes [latex]20 \text{KB}, 4 \text{KB}[/latex], [latex]25 \text{KB}, 18 \text{KB}, 7 \text{KB}, 9 \text{KB}, 15 \text{KB}[/latex], and [latex]12\text{KB}[/latex]. Assume that no two holes are adjacent. Two processes [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] of size [latex]16KB[/latex] and [latex]\text{P2}[/latex] of size [latex]9KB[/latex] arrive in that order, and they are allocated memory using the best-fit technique. After allocating space to [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{P2}[/latex], the number of holes of size less than [latex]8KB[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer) Note: [latex]1 {K}=2^{10}[/latex]
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: Best-fit always picks the smallest hole that is still large enough to satisfy the request. Initial holes (KB): [latex]20,4,25,18,7,9,15,12[/latex]. P1 (16 KB): smallest hole [latex]\ge16[/latex] is [latex]18[/latex]. Allocate there, leaving a remainder hole of [latex]18-16=2[/latex] KB. Holes become: [latex]20,4,25,7,9,15,12,2[/latex]. P2 (9 KB): smallest hole [latex]\ge9[/latex] is the exact-fit [latex]9[/latex] KB hole itself, which is fully consumed (disappears entirely). Holes become: [latex]20,4,25,7,15,12,2[/latex] ([latex]7[/latex] holes remaining). Counting holes smaller than [latex]8[/latex] KB among [latex]\{20,4,25,7,15,12,2\}[/latex]: [latex]4[/latex] KB, [latex]7[/latex] KB, and [latex]2[/latex] KB — exactly [latex]3[/latex] holes. Answer: 3 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523101/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-45#a_list)

question: A system has a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) that has a reach of [latex]1[/latex] MB. TLB reach is defined as the total amount of physical memory that can be accessed through the TLB entries. The paging system uses pages of size [latex]4[/latex] KB. The virtual address space is [latex]64[/latex] GB and physical address space is [latex]1[/latex] GB. If each TLB entry stores a [latex]4[/latex]-bit process id, page number, frame number, and a [latex]2[/latex]-bit control field, then the size of the TLB (in bytes) is ________. (answer in integer) Note: [latex]1 {K}=2^{10}, 1 {M}=2^{20}, 1 {G}=2^{30}[/latex]
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: TLB reach [latex]=[/latex] page size [latex]\times[/latex] number of TLB entries, so number of entries [latex]=\dfrac{1\text{ MB}}{4\text{ KB}}=\dfrac{2^{20}}{2^{12}}=2^8=256[/latex] entries. Virtual address space [latex]=64\text{ GB}=2^{36}[/latex] bytes, so virtual page number [latex]=36-12=24[/latex] bits (page size [latex]4\text{ KB}=2^{12}[/latex]). Physical address space [latex]=1\text{ GB}=2^{30}[/latex] bytes, so frame number [latex]=30-12=18[/latex] bits. Each TLB entry stores: [latex]4[/latex]-bit PID [latex]+[/latex] [latex]24[/latex]-bit page number [latex]+[/latex] [latex]18[/latex]-bit frame number [latex]+[/latex] [latex]2[/latex]-bit control [latex]=4+24+18+2=48[/latex] bits [latex]=6[/latex] bytes per entry. Total TLB size [latex]=256\times6=1536[/latex] bytes. Answer: 1536 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523102/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-44#a_list)
subject: Operating System

question: Consider a system that has a cache memory unit and a memory management unit (MMU). The address input to the cache memory is a physical address. The MMU has a translation lookaside buffer (TLB). Assume that when a page is evicted from the main memory, the corresponding blocks in the cache are marked as invalid. For a given memory reference, which of the following sequences of events can NEVER happen?
options: TLB miss, Page table hit, Cache hit
TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit
TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit
TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache miss
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: A memory reference passes through, in order: TLB → (page table, only if TLB misses) → cache. - TLB miss, Page table hit, Cache hit: possible — TLB doesn't have the mapping, page table does (page is in memory), and the corresponding cache block (whose validity depends on the page being resident) can indeed be valid and hit. Can happen. - TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit: impossible . A TLB hit means the page is currently mapped/resident in memory (TLB entries are only valid for pages currently in memory); it is therefore contradictory for the page table to then report a miss (page not in memory) for that very same page. - TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit: impossible . A page-table miss means the page is not in main memory at all — and the problem states that when a page is evicted, its cache blocks are marked invalid. So if the page isn't in memory, its cache blocks cannot be valid, and a cache hit is impossible. - TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache miss: possible and in fact the expected/consistent sequence when a page is genuinely not resident. Answer: "TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit" and "TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit" can NEVER happen. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523036/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-44#a_list)
subject: Operating System

question: Consider a complete graph [latex]K_{n}[/latex] with [latex]n[/latex] vertices ( [latex]n>4[/latex] ). Note that multiple spanning trees can be constructed over [latex]K_{n}[/latex]. Each of these spanning trees is represented as a set of edges. The Jaccard coefficient between any two sets is defined as the ratio of the size of the intersection of the two sets to the size of the union of the two sets. Which one of the following options gives the lowest possible value for the Jaccard coefficient between any two spanning trees of [latex]K_{n}[/latex] ?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: The Jaccard coefficient between two spanning-tree edge sets is [latex]\dfrac{|E_1\cap E_2|}{|E_1\cup E_2|}[/latex], which reaches its lowest possible value [latex]0[/latex] precisely when the two spanning trees share no edges at all (completely edge-disjoint spanning trees). In [latex]K_n[/latex] for [latex]n>4[/latex], there are more than enough edges ([latex]\binom{n}{2}[/latex] total, versus only [latex]n-1[/latex] needed per spanning tree) to always construct two entirely edge-disjoint spanning trees (this is guaranteed by well-known results on edge-disjoint spanning trees in dense graphs, e.g. via Nash-Williams/Tutte-style constructions). When the intersection is empty, the Jaccard coefficient is exactly [latex]0[/latex], which is also the theoretical minimum possible value for any Jaccard coefficient. Answer: 0 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523120/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-26#a_list)
subject: Algorithms

question: Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be a simple, undirected, edge-weighted graph with unique edge weights. Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees (MST) of [latex]G[/latex] is/are true?
options: In every cycle [latex]C[/latex] of [latex]G[/latex], the edge with the largest weight in [latex]C[/latex] is not in any MST
In every cycle [latex]C[/latex] of [latex]G[/latex], the edge with the smallest weight in [latex]C[/latex] is in every MST
For every vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex], the edge with the largest weight incident on [latex]v[/latex] is not in any MST
For every vertex [latex]v \in V[/latex], the edge with the smallest weight incident on [latex]v[/latex] is in every MST
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: When all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique , and two classical facts (cycle property and cut property) apply: - Cycle property: In any cycle [latex]C[/latex], the edge with the strictly largest weight can never appear in any MST (if it did, removing it and adding any other edge of the cycle would still keep the graph connected but reduce total weight). True. - The claim about the smallest -weight edge of every cycle being in every MST is false in general — a small edge can still be excluded if a smaller alternative path already connects its endpoints via other, even-cheaper edges from elsewhere in the graph (cycle property only rules out the *maximum*, it doesn't force in the minimum in the multi-cycle case with unrelated cycles overlapping). - The claim that the largest -weight edge touching any given vertex [latex]v[/latex] is never in any MST is false — that edge might still be the cheapest way to connect an isolated/far-off part of the graph. - Cut property: For any vertex [latex]v[/latex], consider the cut separating [latex]\{v\}[/latex] from the rest of the graph; the minimum-weight edge crossing this cut (i.e. the cheapest edge incident to [latex]v[/latex]) must belong to every MST, since choosing any costlier edge to connect [latex]v[/latex] instead would strictly increase total weight. True. Answer: The largest-weight edge in every cycle is excluded from every MST; and the smallest-weight edge incident to every vertex is included in every MST. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523041/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-39#a_list)
subject: Algorithms

question: An ISP having an address block [latex]202.16.0.0/15[/latex] assigns a block of [latex]6000[/latex] IP addresses to a client, using the classless internet domain routing (CIDR) super-netting approach. Which of the following address blocks can be assigned by the ISP?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: The ISP's block [latex]202.16.0.0/15[/latex] spans two full class-B-sized blocks: all addresses from [latex]202.16.0.0[/latex] to [latex]202.17.255.255[/latex]. For [latex]6000[/latex] addresses via CIDR super-netting, we need a block with at least [latex]6000[/latex] addresses; a [latex]/19[/latex] prefix gives [latex]2^{32-19}=2^{13}=8192[/latex] addresses, which suffices (a [latex]/20[/latex] would only give [latex]4096<6000[/latex]). A valid [latex]/19[/latex] sub-block must (a) lie entirely within [latex]202.16.0.0[/latex]-[latex]202.17.255.255[/latex], and (b) have its network address aligned to a multiple of [latex]32[/latex] in the relevant octet (since [latex]/19[/latex] leaves [latex]13[/latex] host bits, and [latex]2^{13}=8192=32\times256[/latex] addresses per block, so the 3rd octet must be a multiple of [latex]32[/latex]: [latex]0,32,64,\ldots[/latex]). - [latex]202.16.0.0/19[/latex]: [latex]0[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex], and within range. Valid. - [latex]202.17.64.0/19[/latex]: [latex]64[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex], [latex]202.17.x[/latex] is within the /15 range. Valid. - [latex]202.16.32.0/19[/latex]: [latex]32[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex]. Valid. - [latex]202.17.24.0/19[/latex]: [latex]24[/latex] is not a multiple of [latex]32[/latex] (valid boundaries are [latex]0,32,64,\ldots[/latex]), so this is not a properly aligned [latex]/19[/latex] block. Invalid. Answer: 202.16.0.0/19, 202.17.64.0/19, and 202.16.32.0/19 can be assigned. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523034/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-46#a_list)

question: In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set [latex]\text{F}[/latex] of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by [latex]\text{F}[/latex] is called the closure of [latex]\text{F}[/latex]. To compute the closure of [latex]\text{F}[/latex], Armstrong's Axioms can be applied. Consider [latex]X, Y[/latex], and [latex]Z[/latex] as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong's Axioms are described as follows. Reflexivity: If [latex]Y \subseteq X[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] Augmentation: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex], then [latex]X Z \rightarrow Y Z[/latex] for any Z Transitivity: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] and [latex]Y \rightarrow Z[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Z[/latex] The additional rule of Union is defined as follows. Union: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] and [latex]X \rightarrow Z[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Y Z[/latex] It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: The standard proof of the Union rule ([latex]X\to Y,\,X\to Z\;\Rightarrow\;X\to YZ[/latex]) proceeds as follows: 1. [latex]X\to Y[/latex] (given). By Augmentation (adding [latex]X[/latex] to both sides): [latex]X\to XY[/latex] (using [latex]XX=X[/latex]). 2. [latex]X\to Z[/latex] (given). By Augmentation (adding [latex]Y[/latex] to both sides): [latex]XY\to YZ[/latex]. 3. Combining steps 1 and 2 via Transitivity : [latex]X\to XY[/latex] and [latex]XY\to YZ[/latex] gives [latex]X\to YZ[/latex]. This derivation only ever invokes Augmentation and Transitivity — Reflexivity is never needed anywhere in the chain. So these two rules alone are both necessary (the proof genuinely needs both types of steps) and sufficient (nothing else is required). Answer: Augmentation and Transitivity Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523114/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-32#a_list)
subject: Database Management System

question: In the context of relational database normalization, which of the following statements is/are true?
options: It is always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving [latex]3[/latex]NF decomposition of a relation
It is always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving [latex]1[/latex]NF decomposition of a relation
It is not always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition of a relation
It is not always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving [latex]2[/latex]NF decomposition of a relation
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: Standard relational-normalization theory results: - 3NF: It is a classical theorem that every relation schema has a dependency-preserving (and lossless-join) decomposition into 3NF, via the synthesis algorithm on a minimal cover of the FDs. True. - 1NF: 1NF only requires atomic domains; a relation can always trivially satisfy/preserve 1NF without needing to give up any functional dependency (no decomposition is even forced). True. - BCNF: It is a well-known counterexample-backed result that a dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition is not always possible — achieving BCNF can force us to lose some functional dependency (they can only be checked by joining relations back together, which is expensive/impossible to enforce locally). True (i.e., "not always possible" is a true statement). - 2NF: Since a dependency-preserving 3NF decomposition always exists, and 3NF automatically implies 2NF, a dependency-preserving 2NF decomposition is always achievable too. So "it is not always possible to get a dependency-preserving 2NF decomposition" is false . Answer: Dependency-preserving decompositions always exist for 3NF and for 1NF; it is not always possible for BCNF. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523059/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-21#a_list)

question: A non-pipelined instruction execution unit that operates at [latex]1.6[/latex] GHz clock takes an average of [latex]5[/latex] clock cycles to complete the execution of an instruction. To improve the performance, the system was pipelined with a goal of achieving an average throughput of one instruction per clock cycle. However, it could operate only at [latex]1.2[/latex] GHz due to pipeline overheads. While executing a program in the pipelined design, [latex]30 \%[/latex] of instructions encountered a stall of [latex]2[/latex] cycles due to pipeline hazards. The speed-up obtained by the pipelined design over the non-pipelined one for this program is ________(rounded off to two decimal places) Note: [latex]1 {G}=10^{9}[/latex]
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: Non-pipelined time per instruction [latex]=\dfrac{5\text{ cycles}}{1.6\text{ GHz}}=\dfrac{5}{1.6\times10^9}=3.125[/latex] ns. Pipelined cycle time [latex]=\dfrac{1}{1.2\text{ GHz}}=0.8\overline3[/latex] ns. With an ideal CPI of [latex]1[/latex], but [latex]30\%[/latex] of instructions incurring a [latex]2[/latex]-cycle stall: Average CPI [latex]=0.7\times1+0.3\times(1+2)=0.7+0.9=1.6[/latex] cycles/instruction. Average time per instruction (pipelined) [latex]=1.6\times0.8\overline3=1.3\overline3[/latex] ns. Speedup [latex]=\dfrac{3.125}{1.3\overline3}\approx2.34[/latex]. Answer: 2.34 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523099/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-47#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: The EX stage of a pipelined processor performs the memory read operations for LOAD instructions, and the operations for the arithmetic and logic instructions. Let [latex]t_{E X}[/latex] denote the time taken by the EX stage to perform the operation for an instruction. For each instruction type, the values of [latex]t_{E X}[/latex] and [latex]M[/latex] (the number of instructions of that type in a sequence of [latex]100[/latex] instructions for a program P ), are given in the table below. The duration of the pipeline clock cycle is [latex]1[/latex] nanosecond. Assume that the latch time for the interstage buffers in the pipeline is negligible. [latex] \begin{array}{|l|c|c|} \hline \text{Instruction} & \begin{array}{c} t_{EX}\ \text{in} \\ \text{nanoseconds} \end{array} & M \\ \hline \text{LOAD} & 1.8 & 15 \\ \hline \text{IMUL} & 1.5 & 10 \\ \hline \text{IDIV} & 2.5 & 5 \\ \hline \text{FADD} & 1.7 & 10 \\ \hline \text{FSUB} & 1.7 & 5 \\ \hline \text{FMUL} & 2.8 & 15 \\ \hline \text{FDIV} & 3.2 & 5 \\ \hline \begin{array}{l} \text{All other} \\ \text{instructions} \end{array} & \begin{array}{c} \text{Less than} \\ 1.0 \end{array} & 35 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex] When program [latex]\text{P}[/latex] is executed, the number of clock cycles for which the pipeline is stalled due to structural hazards in the EX stage is ________. (answer in integer)
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: There is a single, shared EX-stage functional unit; only one instruction can occupy the EX stage per clock cycle (of duration [latex]1[/latex] ns). If an instruction's actual execution time [latex]t_{EX}[/latex] exceeds [latex]1[/latex] ns, it must occupy the EX stage for [latex]\lceil t_{EX}\rceil[/latex] clock cycles, causing [latex]\left(\lceil t_{EX}\rceil-1\right)[/latex] structural-hazard stall cycles for every instance of that instruction type. [latex]\begin{array}{l|c|c|c}\text{Type}&t_{EX}&\text{cycles needed}&\text{stalls}\times M\\\hline\text{LOAD}&1.8&2&1\times15=15\\\text{IMUL}&1.5&2&1\times10=10\\\text{IDIV}&2.5&3&2\times5=10\\\text{FADD}&1.7&2&1\times10=10\\\text{FSUB}&1.7&2&1\times5=5\\\text{FMUL}&2.8&3&2\times15=30\\\text{FDIV}&3.2&4&3\times5=15\\\text{Others}&{<}1.0&1&0\times35=0\end{array}[/latex] Total stall cycles [latex]=15+10+10+10+5+30+15+0=95[/latex]. Answer: 95 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523030/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-50#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: Which one of the following dependencies among the register operands of different instructions can cause a data hazard in a pipelined processor?
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: A data hazard occurs when an instruction depends on the result of a nearby instruction that has not yet completed in the pipeline. - Read-after-Write (RAW) : a later instruction tries to read a register before an earlier instruction has written its new value — this is a true/flow dependency, and causes a genuine data hazard in a pipeline. - Write-after-Read (WAR) and Write-after-Write (WAW) are anti-/output-dependencies; they cause hazards only in pipelines that allow out-of-order completion, not in a simple in-order pipeline. - Read-after-Read is not a dependency at all — reads never conflict with each other. Answer: Read-after-write Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523074/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-6#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: A 5-stage instruction pipeline has stage delays of 180, 250, 150, 170, and 250, respectively, in nanoseconds. The delay of an inter-stage latch is 10 nanoseconds. explanation: [Question 4 Explanation: In a [latex]5[/latex]-stage pipeline, the clock cycle time must accommodate the slowest stage plus the inter-stage latch delay: [latex]\max(180,250,150,170,250)+10=250+10=260[/latex] ns per cycle. Total time for [latex]n[/latex] instructions in a pipeline [latex]=(n+k-1)[/latex] cycles, where [latex]k=5[/latex] is the number of pipeline stages (accounting for the initial fill of the pipeline): [latex](1000+5-1)\times260=1004\times260=261{,}040[/latex] ns [latex]=261.04\ \mu[/latex]s. Answer: 261.04 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/460847/gate-cse-2025-set-2-question-46#a_list)

explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: Semaphore [latex]A[/latex] (init [latex]1[/latex]) acts as a mutex guarding the critical section (print "*", increment [latex]X[/latex], and the [latex]X{=}{=}2[/latex] check), so all three processes enter this section one at a time, and exactly one of them (whichever happens to be the second to enter) will see [latex]X{=}{=}2[/latex] and print "[latex]\$[/latex]" then signal [latex]B[/latex]. Since the third process cannot even attempt this section until the second has released [latex]A[/latex] (which only happens after printing "[latex]\$[/latex]"), the global order is forced to always be: [latex]{*},{*},\$,{*}[/latex] — exactly two stars, then the dollar, then the third star. A pattern like [latex]{*}{*}{*}\$[/latex] (three stars before the dollar) can never occur. After the dollar, semaphore [latex]B[/latex] gets exactly one initial permit, which starts a chain: each process that consumes the permit via [latex]\text{Wait}(B)[/latex] prints "[latex]\#[/latex]" and immediately regenerates the next permit via its own [latex]\text{Signal}(B)[/latex], letting the next process through in turn. The remaining ("third") star can interleave with this "[latex]\#[/latex]" chain at any point before that third process itself joins the chain — i.e. before any [latex]\#[/latex], after exactly one [latex]\#[/latex], or after exactly two [latex]\#[/latex]'s (but never after all three, since the third process must complete its own star/critical-section before it can take part in the [latex]\#[/latex] chain at all). Answer: **$*###, **$#*##, and **$##*# are all possible; ***$### is impossible. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523105/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-41#a_list)

```c
function OWNRESOURCE(Resource R)
```
