question: Which of the following can be recurrence relation(s) corresponding to an algorithm with time complexity [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: Solve each recurrence and compare to [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]: - [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+1[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=T(1)+(n-1)\times1=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches. - [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+1[/latex]: by the Master theorem, [latex]a=2,b=2[/latex] so [latex]n^{\log_2 2}=n^1=n[/latex]; since [latex]f(n)=1[/latex] is polynomially smaller than [latex]n[/latex], Case 1 gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches. - [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+n[/latex]: this is the classic merge-sort recurrence, [latex]f(n)=n=n^{\log_2 2}[/latex] exactly (Case 2), giving [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]. - [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+n[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(1+2+\cdots+n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]. Answer: T(n)=T(n-1)+1 and T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 both correspond to Θ(n) algorithms. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523131/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-15#a_list)
subject: Algorithms

question: Consider the following recurrence relations: For all [latex]n>1[/latex], [latex] \begin{array}{l} T_{1}(n)=4 T_{1}\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)+T_{2}(n) \\ T_{2}(n)=5 T_{2}\left(\frac{n}{4}\right)+\Theta\left(\log _{2} n\right) \end{array} [/latex] Assume that for all [latex]n \leq 1, T_{1}(n)=1[/latex] and [latex]T_{2}(n)=1[/latex]. Which one of the following options is correct?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: First solve [latex]T_2(n)=5T_2(n/4)+\Theta(\log_2 n)[/latex]. Here [latex]a=5,\,b=4[/latex], so [latex]n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_4 5}[/latex]. Since [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] is polynomially smaller than [latex]n^{\log_4 5}[/latex] (as [latex]\log_4 5\approx1.16>0[/latex]), by the Master theorem (Case 1): [latex]T_2(n)=\Theta\left(n^{\log_4 5}\right)[/latex]. Now solve [latex]T_1(n)=4T_1(n/2)+T_2(n)[/latex]. Here [latex]a=4,\,b=2[/latex], so [latex]n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_2 4}=n^2[/latex]. The extra term [latex]f(n)=T_2(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_4 5})=\Theta(n^{1.16\ldots})[/latex], which is polynomially smaller than [latex]n^2[/latex] (since [latex]n^2/n^{1.16}=n^{0.84}\to\infty[/latex]). By Master theorem Case 1: [latex]T_1(n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex]. Answer: [latex]T_1(n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex] Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523073/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-7#a_list)
subject: Algorithms

question: Let [latex]L_{1}[/latex] and [latex]L_{2}[/latex] be two languages over a finite alphabet, such that [latex]L_{1} \cap L_{2}[/latex] and [latex]L_{2}[/latex] are regular languages. Which of the following statements is/are always true?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: Given: [latex]L_1\cap L_2[/latex] is regular, and [latex]L_2[/latex] is regular. - [latex]L_1[/latex] regular? Not necessarily — [latex]L_1[/latex] could be an arbitrary (even non-context-free) language whose intersection with a specific regular [latex]L_2[/latex] happens to simplify to something regular; this doesn't pin down [latex]L_1[/latex] itself. Not always true. - [latex]L_1\cup L_2[/latex] regular? Same issue — the union still depends on the unconstrained, potentially irregular parts of [latex]L_1[/latex] outside of [latex]L_2[/latex]. Not always true. - [latex]\overline{L_2}[/latex] context-free? Since [latex]L_2[/latex] is regular, its complement [latex]\overline{L_2}[/latex] is also regular (regular languages are closed under complement), and every regular language is also context-free (regular [latex]\subset[/latex] context-free). Always true. - [latex]L_1[/latex] context-free? No general closure property forces this; [latex]L_1[/latex] could even be undecidable/non-context-free as long as it agrees with [latex]L_2[/latex] on the intersection. Not always true. Answer: [latex]\overline{L_2}[/latex] is context-free. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523039/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-41#a_list)
subject: Theory of Computation

Count subsets of [latex]\{A,B,C,D\}[/latex] containing [latex]\{A,B\}[/latex]: freely choose the remaining [latex]\{C,D\}[/latex] → [latex]2^2=4[/latex] subsets. Count subsets containing [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex]: freely choose the remaining [latex]\{B,D\}[/latex] → [latex]2^2=4[/latex] subsets. Subsets counted twice are those containing both [latex]\{A,B\}[/latex] and [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex], i.e. containing [latex]\{A,B,C\}[/latex]: freely choose remaining [latex]\{D\}[/latex] → [latex]2^1=2[/latex] subsets. By inclusion-exclusion, total superkeys [latex]=4+4-2=6[/latex]. Answer: 6 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523025/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-55#a_list)

question: Let [latex]P, Q, R[/latex] and [latex]S[/latex] be the attributes of a relation in a relational schema. Let [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] indicate functional dependency in the context of a relational database, where [latex]X, Y \subseteq\{P, Q, R, S\}[/latex]. Which of the following options is/are always true?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: Using Armstrong's axioms (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity) to test each claim: - {P,Q}→{R} and {P}→{R}, does {Q}→{R} follow? No — {P}→{R} already implies {P,Q}→{R} by augmentation, so the premises give no information forcing {Q}→{R} to hold. Not always true. - {P,Q}→{R}, does {P}→{R} or {Q}→{R} follow? No — {R} may genuinely require both P and Q together (e.g. R functionally depends on the pair but on neither attribute alone). Not always true. - {P}→{R} and {Q}→{S}, does {P,Q}→{R,S} follow? Yes: augment {P}→{R} with Q to get {P,Q}→{R,Q}; augment {Q}→{S} with P to get {P,Q}→{P,S}; using reflexivity ({R,Q}→{R} and {P,S}→{S}) and transitivity gives {P,Q}→{R} and {P,Q}→{S}; the union rule then gives {P,Q}→{R,S}. Always true. - {P}→{R}, does {P,Q}→{R} follow? Yes, directly by the augmentation axiom (adding Q to the left-hand side of a valid FD keeps it valid). Always true. Answer: {P}→{R},{Q}→{S} ∴ {P,Q}→{R,S}; and {P}→{R} ∴ {P,Q}→{R}. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523060/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-20#a_list)

question: To keep track of free blocks in a file system, one of the two approaches is generally used - using bitmaps (bit vectors) or using linked lists. Consider that the linked list approach is used to keep track of free blocks in a file system. Assume that the disk size is [latex]16[/latex] GB , block size is [latex]2[/latex] KB , and block numbers used are [latex]32[/latex]-bit long. A single pointer of size [latex]4[/latex] bytes is used in each block of the list to point to the next block of the list. The number of blocks required to hold the free disk block numbers is ________. (answer in integer) Note: [latex]1 {K}=2^{10}[/latex] and [latex]1 {G}=2^{30}[/latex]
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: Total disk blocks [latex]=\dfrac{16\text{ GB}}{2\text{ KB}}=\dfrac{16\times2^{30}}{2\times2^{10}}=2^{23}=8{,}388{,}608[/latex] blocks, each needing a [latex]32[/latex]-bit ([latex]4[/latex]-byte) block-number entry to be recorded in the free list. Each list-node (itself one [latex]2\text{ KB}=2048[/latex]-byte block) uses [latex]4[/latex] bytes for the "next" pointer, leaving [latex]2048-4=2044[/latex] bytes for storing free-block-number entries, i.e. [latex]\dfrac{2044}{4}=511[/latex] free-block numbers per list block. Number of list blocks needed [latex]=\left\lceil\dfrac{8{,}388{,}608}{511}\right\rceil=\lceil16416.06\ldots\rceil=16417[/latex]. Answer: 16417 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523103/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-43#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: Consider a hard disk with a rotational speed of [latex]15000[/latex] rpm. The time to move the read/write head from a track to its adjacent track is [latex]1[/latex] millisecond. Initially, the head is on track [latex]0[/latex]. The number of sectors per track is [latex]400[/latex]. The sector size is [latex]1024[/latex] bytes. It is necessary to transfer data from [latex]10[/latex] randomly located sectors in each of the following tracks in the order: [latex]5, 12[/latex] and [latex]7[/latex]. The total time for the data transfer (in milliseconds) from the hard disk is ________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: Rotation time per revolution [latex]=\dfrac{60000\text{ ms}}{15000}=4[/latex] ms, so average rotational latency (half a revolution) [latex]=2[/latex] ms, and time per sector [latex]=\dfrac{4\text{ ms}}{400\text{ sectors}}=0.01[/latex] ms. Seek time (head moves [latex]1[/latex] ms per adjacent track, following the path [latex]0\to5\to12\to7[/latex]): [latex]0\to5[/latex]: [latex]5[/latex] tracks [latex]=5[/latex] ms; [latex]5\to12[/latex]: [latex]7[/latex] tracks [latex]=7[/latex] ms; [latex]12\to7[/latex]: [latex]5[/latex] tracks [latex]=5[/latex] ms. Total seek [latex]=5+7+5=17[/latex] ms. Data transfer per track: since the [latex]10[/latex] sectors needed are randomly located, each individual sector access requires (on average) a fresh rotational latency of [latex]2[/latex] ms before the required sector arrives under the head, plus the [latex]0.01[/latex] ms to actually read it: Per track [latex]=10\times(2+0.01)=20.1[/latex] ms. Over [latex]3[/latex] tracks: [latex]3\times20.1=60.3[/latex] ms. Total time [latex]=[/latex] seek [latex]+[/latex] transfer [latex]=17+60.3=77.3[/latex] ms. Answer: 77.3 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523031/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-49#a_list)
subject: Computer Organization & Architecture

question: Let [latex]G[/latex] be a weighted directed acyclic graph with [latex]m[/latex] edges and [latex]n[/latex] vertices. Given [latex]G[/latex] and a source vertex [latex]s[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], which one of the following options gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm to find the lengths of shortest paths from [latex]s[/latex] to all vertices that are reachable from [latex]s[/latex] in [latex]{G}?[/latex]
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: For a directed acyclic graph (DAG) , the fastest known algorithm for single-source shortest paths uses the following two steps: (1) compute a topological ordering of the vertices in [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] time, then (2) process vertices in that topological order, relaxing every outgoing edge of each vertex exactly once, which takes [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] time in total (this correctly computes shortest paths since, in topological order, all edges into a vertex are relaxed before that vertex is finalized, and no negative cycles can exist in a DAG so ordinary Dijkstra-style priority queues or Bellman-Ford repeated relaxation are unnecessary). This is strictly faster than Dijkstra's [latex]\Theta(m+n\log n)[/latex] (needed only for general graphs with a priority queue) or the [latex]\Theta(nm)[/latex] Bellman-Ford bound (needed for general graphs, possibly with negative edges but no negative cycles) — the DAG structure lets us avoid both. Answer: [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523119/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-27#a_list)
subject: Algorithms

question: Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be an undirected, edge-weighted graph with integer weights. The weight of a path is the sum of the weights of the edges in that path. The length of a path is the number of edges in that path. Let [latex]s \in V[/latex] be a vertex in [latex]G[/latex]. For every [latex]u \in V[/latex] and for every [latex]k \geq 0[/latex], let [latex]d_{k}(u)[/latex] denote the weight of a shortest path (in terms of weight) from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]u[/latex] of length at most [latex]k[/latex]. If there is no path from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]u[/latex] of length at most [latex]k[/latex], then [latex]d_{k}(u)=\infty[/latex]. Consider the statements: S1: For every [latex]k \geq 0[/latex] and [latex]u \in V, d_{k+1}(u) \leq d_{k}(u)[/latex]. S2: For every [latex](u, v) \in E[/latex], if [latex](u, v)[/latex] is part of a shortest path (in terms of weight) from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]v[/latex], then for every [latex]k \geq 0, d_{k}(u) \leq d_{k}(v)[/latex]. Which one of the following options is correct?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: [latex]d_k(u)[/latex] is the shortest-path weight from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]u[/latex] using at most [latex]k[/latex] edges — this is exactly the quantity computed by the Bellman-Ford relaxation process after [latex]k[/latex] rounds. S1: [latex]d_{k+1}(u)\le d_k(u)[/latex] — allowing one extra edge of "budget" can only give access to more paths (a path of length [latex]\le k[/latex] is also a path of length [latex]\le k+1[/latex]), so the shortest weight can only stay the same or decrease. True , always. S2: Suppose [latex](u,v)[/latex] lies on a shortest path from [latex]s[/latex] to [latex]v[/latex]; then [latex]d(v)=d(u)+w(u,v)\ge d(u)[/latex] in the limit, so eventually [latex]d_k(u)\le d_k(v)[/latex] once [latex]k[/latex] is large enough. But for small [latex]k[/latex] this need not hold: it's possible that [latex]u[/latex] has not yet been reached with a short enough path (so [latex]d_k(u)=\infty[/latex] is even bigger) or, more subtly, that a different, cheaper path of length [latex]\le k[/latex] to [latex]v[/latex] exists that doesn't go through [latex]u[/latex] at all — the inequality can fail for some particular [latex]k[/latex] even though it eventually holds in the limit. So S2 is not always true for every [latex]k[/latex] . Answer: Only S1 is true. Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523049/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-31#a_list)

question: Consider an array [latex]A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31][/latex]. Suppose the merge sort algorithm is executed on array [latex]A[/latex] to sort it in increasing order. The merge sort algorithm will carry out a total of [latex]7[/latex] merge operations. A merge operation on sorted left array [latex]L[/latex] and sorted right array [latex]R[/latex] is said to be void if the output of the merge operation is the elements of array [latex]L[/latex] followed by the elements of array [latex]R[/latex]. The number of void merge operations among these [latex]7[/latex] merge operations is ________. (answer in integer)
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: A merge is void when every element of the left sub-array is already [latex]\le[/latex] every element of the right sub-array, so the merge simply concatenates them with no interleaving. Trace merge sort on [latex]A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31][/latex]: Bottom level (pairs): [latex][10],[7]\to[7,10][/latex] (result is [latex]R[/latex] then [latex]L[/latex], not "[latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex]") — not void . [latex][8],[19]\to[8,19][/latex] (already [latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex] as-is) — void . [latex][41],[35]\to[35,41][/latex] — not void . [latex][25],[31]\to[25,31][/latex] (already in order) — void . Next level (quads): [latex][7,10]+[8,19]\to[7,8,10,19][/latex] (interleaved, not simply [latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex]) — not void . [latex][35,41]+[25,31]\to[25,31,35,41][/latex] (interleaved) — not void . Final merge: [latex][7,8,10,19]+[25,31,35,41][/latex]: every element of the left ([latex]\le19[/latex]) is already smaller than every element of the right ([latex]\ge25[/latex]), so the merge is simply [latex]L[/latex] followed by [latex]R[/latex] — void . Total merges [latex]=4+2+1=7[/latex] (matches the given count), with exactly [latex]3[/latex] of them void. Answer: 3 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523124/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-22#a_list)

question: Consider a new TCP connection between a sender and a receiver. The receiver advertised window is constant at [latex]48[/latex] KB, the maximum segment size (MSS) is [latex]2[/latex] KB, and the slow start threshold for TCP congestion control is [latex]16[/latex] KB. Assume that there are no timeouts or duplicate acknowledgements. The number of rounds of transmission required for the congestion control algorithm of the TCP connection to reach the congestion avoidance phase is ________. (answer in integer) Note: [latex]1 {~K}=2^{10}[/latex]
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: In TCP slow start, [latex]\text{cwnd}[/latex] starts at [latex]1[/latex] MSS and doubles every round-trip, until it reaches the slow-start threshold ([latex]\text{ssthresh}=16[/latex] KB), at which point congestion avoidance begins. [latex]\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Round}&\text{cwnd}\\\hline1&2\text{ KB (1 MSS)}\\2&4\text{ KB}\\3&8\text{ KB}\\4&16\text{ KB}\end{array}[/latex] At the end of round [latex]4[/latex], [latex]\text{cwnd}[/latex] reaches exactly [latex]16[/latex] KB, equal to [latex]\text{ssthresh}[/latex] — so it takes [latex]4[/latex] rounds of slow-start doubling before the connection is ready to switch into the congestion-avoidance phase. Answer: 4 Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523098/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-48#a_list)
subject: Computer Networks

question: A TCP sender successfully establishes a connection with a TCP receiver and starts the transmission of segments. The TCP congestion control mechanism's slow-start threshold is set to [latex]10000[/latex] segments. Assume that the round-trip time is fixed at [latex]1[/latex] millisecond. Assume that the sender always has data to send, the segments are numbered from [latex]1[/latex], and no segment is lost. Let [latex]t[/latex] denote the time (in milliseconds) at which the transmission of segment number [latex]2000[/latex] starts. Which one of the following options is correct?
explanation: [Question 2 Explanation: In slow start, the congestion window (in segments) doubles every RTT, starting from [latex]1[/latex] segment, as long as it stays below the threshold ([latex]10000[/latex], which is far above anything we'll reach here). [latex]\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{RTT (start time, ms)}&\text{cwnd (segments sent)}&\text{Segment numbers sent}\\\hline0&1&1\\1&2&2\text{-}3\\2&4&4\text{-}7\\3&8&8\text{-}15\\4&16&16\text{-}31\\5&32&32\text{-}63\\6&64&64\text{-}127\\7&128&128\text{-}255\\8&256&256\text{-}511\\9&512&512\text{-}1023\\10&1024&1024\text{-}2047\end{array}[/latex] Segment number [latex]2000[/latex] falls in the batch sent starting at time [latex]t=10[/latex]ms (the [latex]1024[/latex]-[latex]2047[/latex] range). Answer: [latex]10\le t<11[/latex] Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523046/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-34#a_list)
subject: Computer Networks

question: With respect to a TCP connection between a client and a server, which one of the following statements is true?
options: The client and server use a two-way handshake mechanism before the start of data transmission
The server cannot initiate closing of the connection before the client initiates closing of the connection
The client and server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time
explanation: [Question 3 Explanation: Checking each statement about a TCP connection: - TCP uses a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), not a two-way handshake — false. - Either side (client or server) is free to initiate connection termination first; the server is not required to wait for the client — false. - TCP is a full-duplex protocol — data can flow in both directions simultaneously — so "half-duplex" is false. - TCP supports simultaneous close : both client and server can send a FIN at (roughly) the same time, and each independently acknowledges the other's FIN. This is a valid connection-termination scenario in TCP's state machine. Answer: The client and server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523072/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-8#a_list)

question: Consider a relational database schema with two relations [latex]R(P, Q)[/latex] and [latex]S(X, Y)[/latex]. Let [latex]E=\{\langle u\rangle \mid \exists v \exists w\langle u, v\rangle \in R \wedge\langle v, w\rangle \in S\}[/latex] be a tuple relational calculus expression. Which one of the following relational algebraic expressions is equivalent to [latex]E[/latex] ?
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: The calculus expression [latex]E=\{\langle u\rangle \mid \exists v\,\exists w\,\langle u,v\rangle\in R \wedge \langle v,w\rangle\in S\}[/latex] asks for all [latex]u[/latex] such that some tuple [latex]\langle u,v\rangle[/latex] is in [latex]R[/latex] and that same [latex]v[/latex] appears as the first component of some tuple [latex]\langle v,w\rangle[/latex] in [latex]S[/latex]. This is a natural join of [latex]R[/latex] and [latex]S[/latex] where [latex]R[/latex]'s second attribute ([latex]Q[/latex], which plays the role of [latex]v[/latex]) matches [latex]S[/latex]'s first attribute ([latex]X[/latex], which also plays the role of [latex]v[/latex]): join condition [latex]R.Q=S.X[/latex]. After joining, we only want the value of [latex]u[/latex], i.e. project onto [latex]P[/latex]. So [latex]E\equiv\Pi_P\big(S\bowtie_{S.X=R.Q}R\big)[/latex] (the join is symmetric, so writing [latex]S[/latex] first or [latex]R[/latex] first with the same condition gives the same relation). Answer: [latex]\Pi_P\left(S\bowtie_{S.X=R.Q}R\right)[/latex] Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523047/gate-cse-2026-set-1-question-33#a_list)

options: Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] halts on all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}[/latex]
Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] accepts all input strings in [latex]L[/latex]
Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] rejects all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}-L[/latex]
Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] accepts all input strings in [latex]L[/latex] and rejects all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}-L[/latex]
explanation: [Question 1 Explanation: A Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] "decides" a language [latex]L[/latex] means [latex]M[/latex] is a total decider for [latex]L[/latex]: it must halt on every input, and its halting outcome must correctly classify membership — accepting every string that is in [latex]L[/latex], and rejecting every string that is not in [latex]L[/latex] (i.e. every string in [latex]\{0,1\}^*-L[/latex]). Simply halting on all inputs (without specifying correct accept/reject behavior) isn't enough by itself, and neither "accepts all of [latex]L[/latex]" nor "rejects all of the complement" alone captures the full requirement (each addresses only one direction). Only the combination of both conditions together is equivalent to "decides [latex]L[/latex]." Answer: M accepts all strings in L and rejects all strings in {0,1}*-L Click here for detail solution](https://gateoverflow.in/523143/gate-cse-2026-set-2-question-3#a_list)
